experiments.title: Kafka Consumer Offset Commit Race
experiments.subtitle: Rebalance mid-batch causes uncommitted offsets to be reprocessed
experiments.scenario: A payment processing service uses manual offset commits (enable.auto.commit=false) to guarantee delivery. When the service is slow, a group rebalance reassigns the partition before commitSync() is called — causing the new consumer to reprocess the same payment records.
experiments.impact: Duplicate payment debits reach end-users; reconciliation gaps inflate daily settlement totals and trigger fraud alerts.

experiments.failureExplanation: Kafka's group coordinator triggers a rebalance when a consumer exceeds max.poll.interval.ms without polling. If the batch takes longer than that interval to process, the coordinator revokes the partition and assigns it to another consumer before commitSync() executes. Because no offsets were committed, the new consumer starts from the last committed offset and reprocesses every record the original consumer already handled.

assessment.text: Why does placing commitSync() at the end of a batch create a duplicate-processing risk in Kafka?
options: A) Kafka automatically commits offsets every 5 seconds regardless of manual commits
B) A rebalance between the last process() call and commitSync() leaves all batch offsets uncommitted, so the new owner replays them
C) commitSync() blocks the event loop, causing the broker to drop the partition
D) Kafka only allows one commitSync() per consumer session
assessment.explanation: Kafka's at-least-once guarantee means uncommitted offsets are redelivered after a rebalance. If commitSync() has not been called when the partition is revoked, the new consumer starts from the last committed offset and reprocesses all records the original consumer already handled.

assessment.text: Which configuration parameter controls how long a Kafka consumer can be absent from poll() before the coordinator considers it dead and triggers a rebalance?
options: A) session.timeout.ms
B) heartbeat.interval.ms
C) max.poll.interval.ms
D) fetch.max.wait.ms
assessment.explanation: max.poll.interval.ms defines the maximum delay between successive poll() calls. If the consumer exceeds this interval — typically because processing is too slow — the coordinator triggers a rebalance and revokes its partitions, even if the heartbeat thread is still running.

assessment.text: What is the primary trade-off of Kafka Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS) compared to per-record commitSync()?
options: A) EOS requires Zookeeper; per-record commit works with KRaft mode only
B) EOS delivers ~20% lower throughput but eliminates application-level deduplication logic entirely
C) EOS only works with Avro serialisation; JSON is unsupported
D) EOS commits offsets synchronously on every record just like commitSync()
assessment.explanation: Kafka EOS uses producer transactions to atomically commit offsets and produced messages, providing true exactly-once guarantees. The overhead of two-phase commit and zombie fencing reduces throughput by roughly 20% compared to at-least-once delivery, but it removes the need for idempotency keys at the application layer.

experiments.title: Zombie Consumer After Group Rebalance
experiments.subtitle: Network partition keeps a stale consumer alive — two pods process the same payments
experiments.scenario: A Kafka payment consumer crashes internally but its TCP connection to the broker stays open due to a network partition. The coordinator's session timer expires and it reassigns the partition to a healthy consumer. The zombie then resumes polling and both consumers process the same payment records simultaneously.
experiments.impact: Duplicate payment debits are issued; account balances go negative; fraud detection triggers false positives that freeze merchant accounts.

experiments.failureExplanation: When a network partition isolates a consumer, its TCP connection remains open so the heartbeat thread continues sending heartbeats — the coordinator never sees a session timeout. If the application thread stops calling poll() due to an internal crash, the coordinator waits for max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes by default) before declaring the consumer dead and triggering a rebalance. During this window both the zombie and the newly assigned consumer may poll the same partition.

assessment.text: What condition allows a zombie Kafka consumer to continue sending heartbeats even after its application thread has crashed?
options: A) The consumer automatically spawns a backup heartbeat process on crash
B) Kafka brokers ignore heartbeat failures for the first 60 seconds
C) The heartbeat runs on a separate background thread; a crashed application thread does not kill it, so the TCP connection and heartbeats persist
D) The consumer commits offsets automatically, keeping the session alive
assessment.explanation: Kafka's consumer client separates the heartbeat thread from the application polling thread. If the application thread crashes or stalls without killing the JVM process, the heartbeat thread continues sending heartbeats independently, so the coordinator never sees a session timeout and the zombie retains partition ownership.

assessment.text: Which configuration change most directly shrinks the zombie consumer window in a Kafka consumer group?
options: A) Increase max.poll.records to process fewer batches
B) Decrease session.timeout.ms so the coordinator detects the dead consumer faster
C) Increase fetch.min.bytes to reduce polling frequency
D) Set auto.offset.reset=earliest to replay from the beginning
assessment.explanation: session.timeout.ms controls how long the coordinator waits after the last successful heartbeat before declaring a consumer dead and triggering a rebalance. Lowering it from 30s to 6s reduces the zombie window by 80%, limiting the period during which two consumers can own the same partition.

assessment.text: Why is an idempotency guard (database unique constraint on payment_id) described as 'defence-in-depth' rather than a primary fix for the zombie consumer problem?
options: A) Database constraints cannot prevent duplicate Kafka consumption
B) The guard adds latency that makes Kafka consumers slower than the zombie timeout
C) It prevents the symptom (duplicate debit) but not the root cause (dual partition ownership); proper timeout tuning and fencing must eliminate the zombie first
D) Unique constraints only work with relational databases, not NoSQL stores
assessment.explanation: An idempotency guard prevents the harmful outcome of zombie consumption (a duplicate financial transaction) but does not stop the zombie from consuming records, holding partition ownership, or skewing consumer lag metrics. Proper session timeout tuning and generation-id fencing address the root cause by evicting the zombie and rejecting its subsequent poll attempts.

experiments.title: Redis Cache Stampede on Balance Read
experiments.subtitle: Simultaneous cache expiry floods PostgreSQL and returns stale balances
experiments.scenario: Account balances are cached in Redis with a 60-second TTL. At the moment of expiry, 1,000 concurrent API requests all miss the cache simultaneously, all query PostgreSQL, and all attempt to repopulate Redis — the database is overwhelmed and some requests return stale or inconsistent balances.
experiments.impact: PostgreSQL connection pool exhaustion causes payment authorization timeouts; some accounts temporarily show incorrect available balances, leading to declined transactions or overdrafts.

All threads see null, all issue a database query in parallel, and all write back to Redis — a classic thundering herd. Because the PostgreSQL connection pool has a fixed size, the simultaneous queries exhaust available connections, forcing later requests to queue or timeout.

assessment.text: What causes a cache stampede in a Redis-backed balance service?
options: A) Redis running out of memory and evicting keys under LRU policy
B) Multiple threads simultaneously reading a key that just expired, all missing the cache and issuing redundant database queries
C) The database returning different values to different threads due to read isolation
D) Redis replication lag causing primary and replica to return different values
assessment.explanation: A cache stampede occurs when a TTL expiry causes every concurrent thread to see a cache miss at the same instant. Without coordination, all threads independently query the database and attempt to repopulate the cache, overwhelming the database and defeating the caching strategy.

assessment.text: What is the purpose of the double-checked read (re-reading the cache inside the lock) in the Redisson single-flight pattern?
options: A) To verify that the Redisson lock was acquired correctly
B) To ensure the balance returned is always the most recent value from the database
C) To avoid a database query if another thread already populated the cache while the current thread was waiting for the lock
D) To prevent Redis from accepting stale writes from other pods
assessment.explanation: Threads that were queued waiting for the lock check the cache again after acquiring it. The first thread to acquire the lock will find the cache empty and query the database. All subsequent threads will find the cache already populated by the first thread and return immediately without hitting the database.

assessment.text: How does adding TTL jitter (e.g., 55–65 seconds instead of a fixed 60 seconds) reduce cache stampede risk?
options: A) It increases the total time data stays in cache, reducing miss frequency
B) It staggers expiry times across different cache keys and pod write times, so not all keys expire simultaneously
C) It instructs Redis to automatically refresh keys before they expire
D) It prevents any two threads from writing to the same Redis key within the jitter window
assessment.explanation: TTL jitter spreads expiry events across a time window rather than concentrating them at a single point. When millions of keys all have TTL=60s exactly, they expire together and cause a simultaneous stampede. With jitter, different keys expire at slightly different times, distributing the resulting DB load evenly across the jitter window.

experiments.title: Distributed Lock Expiry During Financial Operation
experiments.subtitle: Redisson TTL shorter than processing time allows a second pod to acquire the lock — duplicate payment
experiments.scenario: Payment deduplication relies on a Redisson distributed lock with a 5-second TTL. When a slow downstream payment gateway causes processing to take 6 seconds, the lock expires before unlock() is called. A second pod then acquires the lock and processes the same payment, issuing a duplicate transaction.
experiments.impact: Customers are charged twice for the same transaction; chargeback rates increase; card network fines are triggered when duplicate-transaction rates exceed thresholds.

assessment.text: What is Redisson's watchdog, and what problem does it solve?
options: A) A monitoring thread that alerts on Redis connection failures
B) A background daemon that periodically renews a lock's TTL while the holder JVM is alive, preventing auto-expiry during long operations
C) A circuit breaker that prevents new lock acquisitions when Redis is overloaded
D) A fallback that acquires a local JVM lock when Redis is unavailable
assessment.explanation: Redisson's watchdog is an internal scheduled task that calls PEXPIRE on a lock key every lockWatchdogTimeout/3 milliseconds, resetting the TTL and preventing auto-expiry. It activates only when lock.lock() is called without an explicit leaseTime, and it stops when lock.unlock() is called or the JVM process terminates.

assessment.text: Why does specifying an explicit leaseTime in lock.lock(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) disable the Redisson watchdog?
options: A) Redisson cannot run the watchdog and a TTL simultaneously due to a Redis limitation
B) An explicit leaseTime signals that the caller has intentionally set a maximum lock duration, so Redisson respects that boundary and disables automatic renewal
C) The watchdog requires a Redisson cluster configuration; it does not work with single-node Redis
D) Explicit TTL locks are stored in a separate Redis keyspace where the watchdog has no access
assessment.explanation: Redisson interprets an explicit leaseTime as a deliberate upper bound set by the application. If the caller specifies leaseTime, Redisson assumes they want the lock to expire at that time regardless of operation status and disables watchdog renewal. Omitting leaseTime (-1 internally) enables watchdog mode.

assessment.text: If a JVM hosting a Redisson watchdog lock crashes mid-operation, how does the lock eventually become available?
options: A) The lock is permanently orphaned and must be manually deleted from Redis
B) Redisson on another pod detects the crash and releases the lock within 1 second
C) The watchdog stops renewing the TTL when the JVM dies, so Redis auto-expires the key after the last-renewed TTL (default up to 30 seconds)
D) The lock is released immediately because Redis monitors JVM process health
assessment.explanation: The watchdog runs inside the holder's JVM. When the JVM crashes, the watchdog thread stops and can no longer renew the lock TTL. Redis then auto-expires the key after the last renewed TTL elapses (up to lockWatchdogTimeout, default 30 seconds), after which another node can acquire the lock. This is safer than a permanent orphan but means retries must wait up to 30 seconds after a crash.

experiments.title: CDC Reconciliation Gap (Duplicate Event Redelivery)
experiments.subtitle: Debezium connector restart causes at-least-once redelivery — reconciliation totals are double-counted
experiments.scenario: A Debezium CDC connector captures transaction events from PostgreSQL and publishes them to Kafka. During a network blip, the connector restarts and redelivers events between the last committed Kafka offset and the restart point. A reconciliation job consuming these events double-counts redelivered event pairs, producing incorrect daily closing balances.
experiments.impact: Daily settlement reports show inflated transaction totals, triggering regulatory reconciliation failures and requiring manual correction that delays end-of-day processing by hours.

assessment.text: Why does Debezium deliver the same CDC event more than once after a connector restart?
options: A) Debezium uses exactly-once delivery by default; duplicates indicate a misconfiguration
B) Debezium provides at-least-once delivery — it replays from the last committed Kafka offset on restart, which may be before events already captured and sent before the restart
C) The PostgreSQL WAL deletes events after delivery, so Debezium must re-read from the beginning of the log
D) Debezium deduplicates events using the transaction ID, so duplicates are impossible
assessment.explanation: Debezium is an at-least-once delivery system. It periodically commits its Kafka consumer offsets, but the gap between the last committed offset and the actual position at restart causes all events in that gap to be redelivered. Consumers must be idempotent to handle this correctly.

assessment.text: What SQL pattern makes a reconciliation INSERT idempotent against CDC event redelivery?
options: A) INSERT IGNORE INTO reconciliation_events ...
B) INSERT INTO reconciliation_events ... ON CONFLICT (tx_id, event_type) DO NOTHING
C) MERGE INTO reconciliation_events WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET amount=amount
D) INSERT INTO reconciliation_events ... IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reconciliation_events WHERE tx_id=?)
assessment.explanation: PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING clause combined with a unique index on (tx_id, event_type) makes the INSERT atomic and idempotent: if a row with the same key already exists, the statement completes successfully with zero rows inserted rather than raising a duplicate-key error. The rowcount return value lets the application decide whether to update dependent aggregates.

assessment.text: What is the key advantage of the Outbox Pattern over relying solely on CDC idempotency for financial reconciliation?
options: A) The outbox pattern eliminates the need for a Kafka broker entirely
B) Events are written atomically with the business transaction, guaranteeing each business event produces exactly one outbox row — there are no spurious CDC events to deduplicate
C) The outbox pattern uses batch inserts, which are faster than individual CDC events
D) The outbox pattern automatically retries failed events without consumer intervention
assessment.explanation: With the Outbox Pattern, the outbox row is inserted in the same database transaction as the business operation. This guarantees that each business event produces exactly one outbox row; Debezium then captures and delivers each row at least once, but the unique event_id on the outbox row makes consumer deduplication trivial. The result is a strongly ordered, deduplicated event stream that reflects exactly the business transactions that committed.

experiments.title: Rate Limiter Race Under Concurrent Pressure
experiments.subtitle: Redis INCR + EXPIRE race allows excess requests to bypass merchant rate limits
experiments.scenario: A merchant API enforces a rate limit of 100 requests per minute using Redis INCR + EXPIRE. Under a burst of 200 concurrent requests, 10 threads all increment the counter before any EXPIRE is set. The counter reaches 110 before EXPIRE fires, allowing 10 extra requests to slip through the limit and triggering downstream fraud scoring at an unsupported rate.
experiments.impact: Merchants can inadvertently bypass rate-limit controls designed to prevent fraud pattern detection; downstream payment processors throttle the platform and issue penalty fees for excessive call rates.

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: redis.incr() and redis.expire() are separate round-trips — another thread can call incr() after the count becomes 1 but before expire() sets the TTL

UNSAFE: count can exceed LIMIT between INCR and EXPIRE because the counter window does not close — 10 extra requests slip through before the key gets a TTL

experiments.failureExplanation: Redis commands are individually atomic but INCR and EXPIRE are separate operations with no guarantee of sequential execution between threads. When 10 threads call INCR simultaneously, they all receive a return value of 1–10 before any EXPIRE is set. Only the thread that received exactly 1 will call EXPIRE; threads receiving 2–10 do not. In the window between all those INCRs and the eventual EXPIRE call, more threads continue to INCR — pushing the counter to 110 — and all are allowed through because the counter has not yet been windowed.

assessment.text: Why does the INCR + EXPIRE pattern fail under concurrent burst traffic in Redis?
options: A) Redis cannot handle more than one INCR command per second per key
B) INCR and EXPIRE are separate commands; between the INCR returning 1 and the EXPIRE call, other threads can INCR the key to values > 1 without a TTL being set, allowing a burst to exceed the limit
C) Redis automatically expires keys after INCR if no EXPIRE is set within 1 second
D) EXPIRE resets the counter to 0, causing the limit to be re-evaluated incorrectly
assessment.explanation: Redis commands are individually atomic but not composed atomically. After the first INCR returns 1, there is a gap before EXPIRE is called. During this gap, all other concurrent threads can INCR the key beyond 1 without any TTL being set. These threads see count > 1 and skip the EXPIRE call, leaving the key windowless until the first thread's EXPIRE executes — by which time the counter may already exceed the limit.

assessment.text: How does executing INCR and EXPIRE inside a Redis Lua script guarantee atomicity?
options: A) Lua scripts run in a separate Redis thread with higher priority than regular commands
B) Redis executes Lua scripts in its single-threaded event loop without preemption — no other command can run between any two operations within the script
C) Lua scripts lock the entire Redis instance for 100ms, preventing concurrent access
D) Redis replicates Lua scripts before execution, making them durable and atomic
assessment.explanation: Redis's execution model is single-threaded for command processing. When a Lua script is submitted via EVAL, Redis runs the entire script to completion before processing any other command. This means the INCR and conditional EXPIRE inside the script execute as a single indivisible unit from the perspective of all other clients.

assessment.text: What is a key operational difference between a fixed-window rate limiter (INCR + EXPIRE) and a token bucket (Bucket4j)?
options: A) Token buckets support higher throughput because they do not use Redis

B) Fixed-window limiters reset the count at exact window boundaries, allowing a burst of 2× the limit across the boundary; token buckets smooth traffic with continuous refill, limiting true burst capacity
C) Token buckets count requests in reverse, decrementing from the limit to zero
D) Fixed-window limiters use Lua scripts while token buckets use transactions
assessment.explanation: A fixed-window limiter with a 1-minute window allows up to 100 requests in the last second of minute N and 100 more in the first second of minute N+1 — a 200-request burst in 2 seconds. A token bucket refills at a steady rate (e.g., 100/60 tokens per second) and limits instantaneous burst capacity, making it more suitable for protecting downstream services from sudden spikes.
